en: According to the system of those who know the tradition, the status of being a lineage-holder (sampradāyitva) arises through receiving initiation and mantra from the lineage-guru (sampradāyiguru). (1)
Indeed, it is only the mantras taught by the teachers of the lineage of the learned that are known as "tradition" (sampradāya) by the wise followers of tradition. (2)
Being a cultured person (*śiṣṭa*) means accepting the authority of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*).
Because the Vedas proclaim the supremacy of Viṣṇu, one who [accepts this] is called a Vaiṣṇava *śiṣṭa*. (3)

Vaishnavahood is not established by that which is not directed toward the Supreme Lord, because it contradicts the scriptures, as stated in passages such as "by one instructed by a non-Vaishnava," and so forth. 4.
Therefore, desiring to preserve the tradition of those instructed by the learned, Gaura—though he was the Veda itself breathed forth from his own mouth—adopted the Mādhva doctrine. (5)
The illustrious Gaurāṅga, the teacher of the entire world, for the sake of instructing the people, made the Lord of the City his guru and accepted the spiritual lineage. (6)
Even some particular views of the proponents of reality have been refuted by the illustrious Gaurāṅgadeva; what, then, is the use of that [refutation] for the tradition? (7)

For those who have received initiation into a single tradition, there may arise only a slight difference of opinion among themselves due to various branches; however, the tradition itself is not divided. 8.
Just as Rāmānandī is included within the Rāmānujīya [tradition], so too are Harivyāsa and others within the Nimbārka sampradāya. 9.
The Gauḍīya exponent of the truth and likewise the follower of the Mādhva doctrine have both entered [the path];
indeed, no contradiction is perceived here by those most proficient in the knowledge of reality. (10)
Even according to the view that "may [the Lord] be pleased," in the determination of the tradition,
if the analysis of the probandum and so forth is accepted as a means of proof,
nevertheless, there is no absolute difference between the views of Śrī-Gaura and Mādhva. (11)
Furthermore, that liberation which is proclaimed as the goal in the Madhva system has been shown by the authors of the Bhāṣya to consist in the attainment of the feet of Viṣṇu. (12)
Madhva accepted the means of attainment (*sādhana*) according to the distinctions of action, the individual soul, and qualification;
yet he also highly praised the superiority of devotion (*bhakti*). (13)
In the Madhva school of thought, the Bhārata alone is the authority; the statement that it is threefold, with verbal testimony as the primary means of knowledge, is false. (14)
How could the Lord of Dvārakā be determined as his chosen deity, by whom the service of the illustrious Nartaka-Gopāla has been firmly established? (15)
Even if Dvārakādhīśa is certain [to be the Lord], what loss is there? He who is Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda, is indeed the Lord of Dvārakā.
There is identity between the two forms; their state as Kṛṣṇa is without distinction. (16)
Due to the distinction between play (līlā) and the conceit of agency (abhimāna), there is the "most full" (pūrṇatama) and the "full" (pūrṇaka);
yet, in terms of their essential nature (svarūpa), no distinction whatsoever exists between the two. (17)

The doctrine of both difference and non-difference, which is called "Inconceivable" (Acintya) by the wise and is well-known among those expert in the Śrī Caitanya school, is indicated within the Madhva system. (18)
Although individual souls (jīvas) are distinct from Brahman due to their being parts of its attributes, they are non-different [from it];
and because they consist of pure consciousness (cinmātra), they possess oneness despite their state of being counter-correlates and their mutual difference. (19)

Due to reasons such as being pervaded by that [the cow] and having a function dependent on that, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the cow-owner and the Madhva priest is the same. (20)
In this system, the skill of mere deliberation regarding power and the possessor of power is called the doctrine of the inconceivable (acintyavāda) by the Gosvāmīs;
the causal doctrine (kāraṇavāda) is said to be primary for the determination of reality. //21//
"Brahman, denoted by the term 'Parā', is the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa);
however, that same Brahman, joined with the powers of the individual soul (jīva) and primordial matter (pradhāna), is the material cause (upādāna).
Thus, even in the doctrine of causality, the views of both [schools] are identical. (22)
If one considers the commentary named *Śrīgovinda* to be authoritative, then this is a compendium extracted from its established conclusions regarding the jewels of objects of knowledge. (23)
If one says at the outset, "Madhva spoke thus," implying he expresses the consensus of Śrī Gaura, or if some overlook this, then the logic of the "half-cock" (ardhakukkuṭi) applies. 24.
Thus it was recorded by the venerable Śrī Haridāsa Dāsa within the illustrious literature of the Śrī Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition.
